Project question

How can sales and purchasing behaviour across a retail network be analysed to inform commercial decisions?

Why this project?

I chose this project to apply my data analysis skills to a commercial question. I wanted to understand sales and purchasing habits and suggest actions to test. It was also an opportunity to develop my Power BI and DAX skills using a large dataset.

Summary and recommendations

What can we learn and which actions could we test?

Customer loyalty

Customers in the ‘Very loyal’ segment account for around 21% of customers and 48.4% of net sales.

Action to test

Offer a loyalty benefit to part of this segment and compare purchases with a control group.

Main markets

The United States and China are the two highest-ranking countries by sales.

Suggested action

Compare the best-selling categories in these two countries to tailor commercial campaigns.

Peak periods

Sales peaks appear towards the end of the year in both 2023 and 2024 shown in the report.

Suggested action

Plan inventory and prepare commercial campaigns ahead of these periods.

Analysis limitations

The data is synthetic and amounts are expressed in US dollars (USD). The results describe observed sales. Profitability and the causal effect of promotions were not evaluated.

My approach

I first checked the quality of the files and prepared a combined table for Power BI. I then used DAX measures to calculate the indicators shown across the report’s eight pages.

See the five preparation and development steps

  1. Exploring the files

    I examined all six tables to understand their contents and relationships. I checked column types, missing values, duplicates and unique values.

  2. Cleaning the data with Python

    I removed 798 duplicates, converted dates and created time variables. I also calculated ages and age groups and translated categories into French. Amounts were converted to USD so countries could be compared using the same unit.

    The conversion used approximate fixed exchange rates.

  3. Building an analysis table

    I joined transactions with products, stores and customers. This flat table brings together the information needed for the report’s visuals and measures.

  4. Creating DAX measures

    I built more than twenty measures to track sales, average purchase amounts and returns. Other calculations compare loyalty segments and sales with and without discounts.

    The same measures are reused across the pages to keep definitions consistent.

  5. Organising the eight pages

    Each page addresses a commercial question. I chose visuals for the type of comparison, then added filters and shared navigation between topics.

See DAX examples and customer segmentation

Calculating net sales

CA Total = CALCULATE(SUM('fashion_dashboard_clean'[Line_Total_USD]), 'fashion_dashboard_clean'[Is_Return] = FALSE())
CA Returns = ABS(CALCULATE(SUM('fashion_dashboard_clean'[Line_Total_USD]), 'fashion_dashboard_clean'[Is_Return] = TRUE()))
CA Net = [CA Total] - [CA Returns]

I separated sales and returns using the column Is_Return created in Python. Net sales are sales after deducting the value of returns.

Defining the return rate

Taux Retour % = DIVIDE([Nb Returns], COUNTROWS('fashion_dashboard_clean')) * 100

This rate is the share of return rows among all sales and return rows. The function DIVIDE handles division by zero.

Measuring the share of discounted transactions

Nb Transactions Avec Discount = CALCULATE([Nb Transactions], 'fashion_dashboard_clean'[Discount] > 0)
Taux Transactions Promotionnelles = DIVIDE([Nb Transactions Avec Discount], [Nb Transactions]) * 100

The measure reuses the transaction count and filters for the presence of a discount. It describes observed discounted sales.

Ranking customers by net sales

Top 10 CA Net = CALCULATE([CA Net], TOPN(10, ALL('fashion_dashboard_clean'[Customer ID]), [CA Net], DESC))

I used TOPN to select the top ten customers by net sales.

Defining loyalty segments

Segmentation uses the number of purchases across the full history loaded into the report.

Occasional · 1 purchase Regular · 2 to 3 purchases Loyal · 4 to 7 purchases Very loyal · 8 or more purchases
See possible extensions to the analysis

I could extend this work with sales forecasting and RFM segmentation. RFM groups customers by how recently they purchased, how often they purchase and how much they spend. Repeating the analysis with real data would also allow me to compare these observations with a real commercial setting.
